newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian suicide just the first, says doctor.
newsitem.headline: Australian suicide just the first, says doctor.

text.p: The Australian doctor who helped out with the world's first legally assisted suicide said on Thursday it opened the way for more such deaths.
"The next one will be easier, it always gets easier," Philip Nitschke told Reuters from Darwin, capital of Australia's remote Northern Territory.

Nitschke helped an unidentified Darwin man in his mid-60s die from a lethal injection on Sunday, nearly three months after the world's first voluntary euthanasia law came into operation in the outback region.
Nitschke, who has watched another patient die in agony while he battled to win approval to use the law, said he had "several" more patients waiting to apply for the right to die.

Winning approval for more assisted suicides would be easier now that the first had happened and the law and structure were in place, said the euthanasia campaigner dubbed Australia's "Doctor Death" by his critics.
The territory law allowing terminally ill patients to end their lives with lethal injections or pills came into operation on July 1.

But Nitschke's efforts to win approval for patients to use the law was first stymied by a series of legal and political challenges which discouraged doctors from supporting his application because of uncertainty about their legal position.
Two doctors and a psychiatrist must support the application and Nitschke had to fly in a psychiatrist from Sydney to approve the Darwin man's application.
Nitschke said the death of former patient Max Bell, 66, from New South Wales state, had made it easier to find the three signatures for the latest case.
Bell, who was in great pain when he died in August, had been unable to convince a psychiatrist to approve his application.
"There has been a reaction to Max Bell's plight," Nitshcke said. "There is a degree of guilt being felt (in the medical profession)."
